I've watched a few videos on YouTube where they demonstrate how to strike stones together in order to create sharp edges or sharp shards. I want to take survivalism skills one piece at a time and start with practicing this skill and building up from it. I'm not sure which stones I should be looking for in this first step however.

Is there anything specific in a stone that I should be looking for to determine how easily or well I can get sharp edges out of it?
Does anyone have advice on which rocks or stones work best to make sharp shards for cutting and knife making?
Obsidian is one of the most favorite if you can find/afford it. The most popular and effective with primitive survivalists, also what native americans used, is chert.

Everybody has seen obsidian at one time or another. Obsidian is common in the volcanic areas of the Western United States. Chert is also common but most people could not pick out a piece of chert in a bunch of rocks to save their souls. Well here are some guidelines. Chert is a sedimentary rock. So don't go looking for chert in a field of granite. But in fields of lime stone you might be in luck. Limestone is a soft form of sedimentary rocks that may (or may not) have nodules or bands of a harder material in it. Chert is common in limestone, chalk, dolostone or other sedimentary formations. Chert most often is found as round boulders that when shattered show the sharp edges that are the desired features of Chert. Chert is common in the Eastern mountain formations but is rare in the west. By the way that chert is very useful is in the making of sharpening stones. What you want to do is keep breaking chert into smaller and smaller pieces, A fine chert dust is what you are looking fore. Then you mix the chert dust with clay and fire it in a kiln. What you get is a ceramic with small pieces of chert embedded in it. It is the chert that removes the metal from a cutting tool as it is drawn across the ceramic block.

Personally the use of stone tools is not optimum but rather a necessity if you are on the move and need to cover ground in a hurry. Steel is a much more preferred material. (Also iron bearing rocks and scrap steel are easy to find) now most iron bearing rocks are not profitable for use in making steel but exist almost every where. It is just a simple mater of concentrating the iron from low iron content rocks. Since almost all rocks have a high silicon content and while Silicon and Iron have roughly the same melting point, Iron is about three times heavier than silicon. When Iron bearing rocks are crushed and place into a sealed ceramic crucible with some charcoal then melted the iron will sink to the bottom. So through many firings you can concentrate Iron up to almost pure form. (The charcoal is necessary to provide as source of Carbon monoxide which is the reducing agent to remove the oxide from iron ore, (fe203 or fe3O4)). Of course with the proper amount of charcoal the carbon of the charcoal will enter the iron ore crystalline structure to make the most magical of all metals STEEL. By the way the making of charcoal from wood when done by destructive distillation also yields many other valuable products, mainly two type of creosote, light wood oil (a valuable preservative) and methyl alcohol. Creosote and methyl alcohol are valuable medicinal products for the control of infections of wounds and injuries. light wood oil can be used for chapped skin, and sun and wind burns. So in a post apocalyptic world the man who can make and work metal would be one of the most valuable persons of a village.
